title: A Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
summary: Defines the Simple Network Management Protocol, a simple way to inspect or change management information on a network element from a remote location. It is a re-release of RFC 1098 with a changed status section. It was a standards-track document and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Network devices have settings and counters. This is a simple way to ask a device what is going on, or tell it to change a setting.

questions: what udp ports does snmp use
subtitle: The original SNMP: a deliberately simple get, set and trap protocol for inspecting and changing network device state.

tldr.problem: TCP/IP networks needed a simple, workable way to inspect and alter management information on hosts, gateways and other network elements from a remote station.
tldr.mechanism: SNMP models management as reading and writing variables. A manager sends GetRequest, GetNextRequest or SetRequest messages, the agent answers with a GetResponse, and the agent can send unsolicited traps. Each message is a single UDP datagram.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1157 was a standards-track document. It is now Historic, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting RFC.

today: RFC 1157 has Historic status, and it obsoletes RFC 1098 as a re-release of it. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Background and Goals
sections.content:
RFC 1157 is a re-release of RFC 1098 with a changed status section and a few typographical corrections. It defines the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), which sits alongside the Structure of Management Information (RFC 1155) and the Management Information Base (RFC 1156) as the framework for managing TCP/IP internets. The IAB recommended that all IP and TCP implementations be network manageable.

The design explicitly minimizes the number and complexity of management functions in the agent. That lowers agent development cost and leaves management tools free to be as sophisticated as they like. The protocol is not backwardly compatible with its predecessor SGMP, and new UDP ports were allocated to avoid confusion.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal was to keep the thing inside each gadget as small and dumb as possible, so all the clever work happens at the manager's desk.

sections.title: The SNMP Architecture
sections.content:
Network management stations run management applications that monitor and control network elements such as hosts, gateways and terminal servers. Each element has an agent that does the work. Everything is modeled as inspecting or altering variables, so the agent needs only two essential functions, get and set. There are no imperative commands. A reboot, for example, could be triggered by setting a parameter holding the number of seconds until reboot.

Monitoring is done mainly by polling, with a limited number of unsolicited traps to guide timing and focus. Only non-aggregate object types are covered. Information is represented in a subset of ASN.1, using only the definite-length form of the basic encoding rules.

Administrative relationships are built from communities, each named by a community name, plus a MIB view and an access mode of READ-ONLY or READ-WRITE. A pairing of a community with a community profile is an access policy. A proxy access policy lets one agent manage devices that cannot speak the protocol directly.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager polls gadgets by asking questions, and only a few urgent things make a gadget speak up on its own. A community name is like a shared password word that says who is asking and what they may touch.

sections.title: Naming Object Instances
sections.content:
Each variable is identified by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER of the form x.y, where x names an object type in the MIB and y identifies the instance. Objects with no special rule use x.0, so sysDescr (1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1) has its single instance at 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0.

Table entries are named by their index, for example ifType.2 for the type of interface 2, or ipAdEntNetMask.89.1.1.42 for the netmask of the interface with address 89.1.1.42. Related variables sit next to each other in lexicographic order, which makes GetNextRequest useful for walking tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Every dial in every gadget has a long numbered address, like a library shelf code. Dials in the same table are shelved side by side, so you can read them one after another.

sections.title: Messages and Operations
sections.content:
A message holds a version identifier, a community name and a PDU, all inside one UDP datagram. Agents receive messages on UDP port 161, and traps go to UDP port 162. An implementation need not accept messages longer than 484 octets. All five PDUs are mandatory.

  • GetRequest retrieves the named variables.
  • GetNextRequest returns the next variable in lexicographic order, which is how tables are traversed.
  • GetResponse carries the answer. Its error-status can be noError(0), tooBig(1), noSuchName(2), badValue(3), readOnly(4) or genErr(5), with error-index pointing at the offending variable.
  • SetRequest assigns values, and the assignments should take effect as if simultaneous.
  • Trap is an unsolicited report from the agent.

A request-id lets a manager match responses to outstanding requests and spot duplicates, which matters because UDP is unreliable.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for a value, ask for the next one, set one, get an answer, or hear an alarm. Each message fits on one postcard, and a numbered ticket matches answers to questions.

sections.title: Traps
sections.content:
A Trap-PDU carries the enterprise object identifier, the sender's agent-addr, a generic-trap code, a specific-trap code, a time-stamp and variable bindings. The generic types are coldStart(0), warmStart(1), linkDown(2), linkUp(3), authenticationFailure(4), egpNeighborLoss(5) and enterpriseSpecific(6).

Implementations must be able to generate the authentication failure trap but must also be able to suppress it. The linkDown and linkUp traps put the affected ifIndex first in the variable bindings.
sections.plainLanguage: A trap is the gadget ringing a bell: I just restarted, a cable came unplugged, or someone tried a wrong password.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content: The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo. The architecture does define an authentication service that decides whether a message is authentic for a community, and the RFC notes that effective management needs services able to identify authentic messages with a high degree of certainty. Some implementations may use a trivial scheme that accepts every message as authentic.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook mostly leaves the question of how to be sure who is asking to other pieces, and allows a very trusting version that believes everyone.

items.desc: Sender is reinitializing; configuration or implementation may change.

items.desc: Sender is reinitializing; neither configuration nor implementation changes.
